title: Giant Carboniferous insects and pterodactyls imply a denser ancient atmosphere

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Giant Carboniferous insects and pterodactyls imply a denser ancient atmosphere

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The giant wingspans of Carboniferous dragonflies and the small bodies and huge wings of pterodactyls, which seem beyond present mechanical limits, can be explained if the Carboniferous and Jurassic atmosphere was notably denser, for example through more carbonic acid.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: we have only to suppose that in carboniferous and jurassic days the terrestrial atmosphere was notably denser than it is at present, by reason, for instance, of its containing a much larger proportion of carbonic acid, and we have at once a means of reconciling the apparent mechanical discrepancy.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter II, “On Magnitude”; topic “Giant fossil fliers and air density”. Scope: Carboniferous giant insects and Jurassic pterosaurs

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch02-08: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.62

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The historical hypothesis has measurable fossil and geochemical consequences and relevant public repositories exist. Sparse atmospheric proxies and uncertain flight reconstructions limit a clean causal test, although substantial parts can be evaluated now.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Combine fossil body and wing reconstructions with independent proxy estimates of atmospheric pressure and composition, then model whether inferred density was required for flight. Modern-density mechanical feasibility or proxies excluding notably greater density would refute the proposed explanation.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Fossil deformation and missing soft tissues affect aerodynamic estimates.

High oxygen, not carbon dioxide, is a major rival explanation for insect gigantism.

Ancient total atmospheric pressure is poorly constrained.

fields.value:

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Fossil sizes and paleo-CO2 compilations are public, so one can ask whether the intervals of giant fliers were intervals of high CO2. That is only a proxy for the stated mechanism, because a higher proportion of carbonic acid need not raise total atmospheric density, and other environmental explanations fit the same fossils. The test can weaken this particular reconciliation; it cannot cleanly confirm denser air.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Place Carboniferous dragonfly and Jurassic pterosaur wingspans and body sizes against mechanical flight limits at modern air density, then ask whether reconstructed atmospheric density in those intervals is high enough to remove the discrepancy. Giants during a low-density interval would count against this explanation; a matching dense interval would support it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Oxygen, temperature, and phylogeny are alternative explanations of giant size.

Many specimens lack paired wingspan and body mass.

Carbon dioxide concentration is not total air density or pressure, which is what the flight calculation uses.
